Grand Ball to the Prince de Joinville, at Boston. þÿ This affair, which came off on Wed- i nesday night last, was conceived and executed in that spirit for which our sister city is i lamous, of never doing things by halves. All the arrangements were perfected with such 1 an entire disregard of expense, that the aggre- j gate cost is stated to have exceeded seven thousand dollars. The þÿ Cradle," as the Bostonians love to call it, was decorated with a great deal of taste with the flags of all civilized nations, each intertwined with our own, and a profusion of bunting. At the head of the Hall a canopy was raised, the back of which was a transparency of þÿ the Belle Pottle," and þÿ I, a þÿGassard' in front was suspended the Star of the Legion of Honor, and above, the arms of France, and on either side, those of the U. In fact, the whole Hall was covered with flowers, innumerable flags, bunting, <fec. and presented, when illuminated by a myriad of lights, a lout þÿensemble of exceeding brilliancy. The company began to arrive at about eight þÿo clock, and at half past nine the Prince and his suit were received in the armory of the Lancers, tastefully fitted up for the occasion, He soon after entered the Hail, now densely crowded with a throng that in magnificence of attire and personal beauty could not be excelled by any city of the Union. After dancing several sets the supper room was thrown open.

The tables were laid in the Rotunda of Quincy Market, a covered bridge connecting the two buildings. The arrangements for the supper were of the most convenient character, the servants all being stationed on the inside next the wall, and the guests in the hollow square fnnned hv the tables extending entirely around the Rotunda. Of the supper it is only neeessaiv to say that the most unbounded profusion was observed, and that the best of each articles that could be procured for money was obtained. After it had sustained the onslaught of fifteen hundred persons, there was enough left to satislv as many more. The wines were of the choicest vintages, and furnished to the guests with the freest prodigality. After remaining in the supper room some time the Prince returned to the Hall, and at about 3 þÿo clock was escorted to his carriage by the Committee. Among the company assembled were a large number of army and navy Officers, and Slate Dignitaries; all the Foreign Consuls who are foreigners.

The hand consisted of forty-eight instruments, and the dancing was kept tip until four þÿo clock. This occasion will he laid up by those who were there, among those pleasant memories which remain with us longest, and we have no doubt the Prince will often remember, when tossed upon the deep, the scene of loveliness presented by Faneuil Hall on Wednesday night þÿ New York Courier and Enquirer, Nov 27.

The Ball, last evening, was the most brilliant affair ever gotten up in Boston. Every thing was in splendid style. The dancing commenced at eight þÿo clock. The noble guest and his suit appeared to enjoy themselves much þÿ were very sociable and agreeable, and were treated with that consideration to which their position entitled them without the exhibition of any vulgar excess of adulation. The ladies looked charmingly þÿ soma of them, the Prince said, were the handsomest he had ever seen ! Their dresses were ail in excellent taste, and many superbly rich. The gentlemen behaved quite well, and generally observed the rules we published yesterday. From the European, Liveopoo! October 21. A cast-iron lighthouse has been constructed by Messrs. Bramah and Robinson, under the direction of Mr. Alexander Gordon, at their manufactory at Pimlico. It is to be erected on the east coast of Jamaica The height from the foundation to the roof is 105 feet, 15 feet of which will be sunk into the solid rook, and loaded in and out with rubble and concrete. 7'he whole tower is formed of iron plates, one inch in thickness, and of these plates there are nine tiers, elevea plates at the bottom and nine at the top ; the whole are bolted together with iron flanges, and when permanently fixed will also be cemented with iron cement, and thus, in effect, become one entire whole. 7'o reduce the heat in the interior, which the strength of a tropical sun acting on a building of metal only one inch in thickness would render unbearable, the whole will have an interior lining of slate, with an interval of one inch and a half between it and the iron, by which a current of air will constantly be in circulation over the whole. The diameter of the tower is 18 feet 6 inches at the base, and decreases at the top to 1 1 feet 6. The entire weight of the whole fabric is exactly 100 tons. This loftlv fabric was erected entirely without the aid of scaffolding, the expense of which, both here and on its final location in Jamaica, would have been very considerable : at present it stands upon the ground, and merely rests on a plane of temporary timber, &c. The manner in which this was effected is

simple : the lower plates were secured together ; a cross beam passed over them, from which a derrick and cradle or windlass were fixed ; by this the second tier of plates was elevated, and thus continued till the whole were placed in a very short time, and very few hands were necessary to effect it. The entrance is elevated from the ground 10 feet and is reached by steps of iron. It is little more than two months since the order was given for the erection of this structure, and it has been some time entirely finished. The whole expense, including the plan, the building, the passage over the Atlantic, and the erecting it, will not exceed, it is said, £7,000. At the top, the platform is a square of 16 feet, which consequently projects over the sides ; this is surrounded by a rail, three feet in height.

From the New York Transcript, November 17, 1841. SPAIN. Scene in a Palacb. þÿ The bold attempt to seize the young Queen of Spain and her sister is one of the most remarkable events, in a small way, of these modern times. It reminds one of the old iron-bound ages, when steel clad barons paid no more respect to royalty than they did to mercy or humanity. 7'he only parallel to it, that occurs to us at the moment, is the slaying of Rizzio in the royal apartments of Mary Queen of Scots. We copied a short account of the affair, on Tuesday from one of the London papers. Here is another, more miuute in its details, from the London Chronicle : þÿ The diabolical attempt of carrying off the Queen from the palace commenced last night. 7'he execution of the plan conducted by Generals Concha, Leou, Duke of San Carlos. ®i.»33£ T33ti»l3K. »3 33a»'JWO-S AT33« Solo, and others, properly began at seven o'clock in the barracks «f the Hussars of the Princess, below the palace. 7'his regiment, which was most faithful, was made prisoners at the moment they were proceeding to take orders at the Duke's residence, by stratagem! Concha, with three companies of the revolted royal guards, came upon all the soldiers in the guard-room, and threatened to fire on them if they stirred His attention being called to another quarter, the officers succeeded in getting to their men and horses, and rendered noble service during the night. Meantime, Concha immediately went to the palace with twelve companies more of the revolted guards, and at once obtained possession of the whole lower part of the palace and grand staircase. The three conipanits of Guards on actual duty at the palace, said to have been bribed, and no doubt truly, ottered no resistance to his entry, but withdrew to the armory, a long building in front of the palace The relieve guard of halberdiers, of about 100 men, had also unfortunately not arrived at the lime ; and the whole defence of the palace and Queen's person, with the Infanta, her sister, devolved upon nineteen old halberdiers, commanded by Col Dulce, a young man of thirty, and nobly did these veterans and theiryoung commander perform their duty. Stationing two men at eachdoor in the seriesof rooms leading to those occupied by the Queen, and placing himself at the first, which he actually left open, he and his brave companions defended themselves

and their royal charge from half past seven o'clock to one when their 1500 assailants had to escape by the Puerta de Hierro, leading toward the Basque provinces. Such was the intensive of the firing kept up by both parties, that the doors, walls and furniture presented the appearance of so many targets, this morning. It would be in vain, even had I time, to attempt to describe the almost superhuman defence made by the brave men to whom Spain is to-day indebted for a Queen. In the dark and confusion of the night, and the occupation of the palace by a large invading force, below in the court yards, assistance from without appears to have been difficult. Fortunately the fate of the Queen did not altogether depend upon it, her safety being in the hands of a few but gallant defenders. On the retreat of Concha at one, hostilities forthemost part terminated, andthe palace was kept possession of till daybreak this morning by the halberdiers. 7'he conduct of Madame Mina was worthy of her name. Most fortunately she too was in the palace with her royal pupils. By conveying them from room to room, asthe bloody battle thickened, she may be said to have in a great degree contributed to their personal safety ; but notwithstanding all her care and firmness, the mark of a bullet was visible this morning on the wall, a few inches above the tied of the Infanta ! Not even to the gallant duke would she open a door, when a moment permitted him to inquire after the safety of his sovereign and her sister.

At daybreak this morning the Duke de la Victoria proceeded, at the head of his escortto the palace. His passage to the palace was among one continuedserics of the loudest and most heartfelt vivals. He visited the Piazza Mayor in his way, and spoke a few words to the people and the troops. He then proceeded to the palace, and fiere a scene of the most interesting and moving kind took place in the presentation of the Royal o phausat

the balcony of ti« palace, to assure the people of the safety of their beloved sovereign. Hundreds were admitted to the Royal apartments to greet and console the Queen and her sister, the latter speaking with infantile simplicity, of herhiding herself to save herself from the balls I 7'lieduke cordially embraced Col. Dulce, and instantly promoted him to the rank of brigadier He next addressed each of the halberdiers separately, and in like manner promoted them, giving them at the same time the laurel cross of San Fernando. 7'hese fine old fellows were at their post wheu the duke entered just as if nothing bad happened. But the most touching scene was, perhaps that of Madame Mina publicly apologizing to Gol. Dulce for her rude denial of admission to bin during the night when he applied to see tiie Queen. The scene and language which passed between both brought tears into the eyes of all present. 1 have thus endeavoured to give you a hurried sketch of the principal events of this most eventfui night. The defection of troops has not, after all, been very considerable. Some companies of the Guards and their officers arc made prisoners. 7'he national Guards and the people conducted themselves with their usual firmness and moderation.

BIRTH OP AN HEIR APPARENT TO THE BRITISH THRONE. The highly gratifying and auspicious event of the birth of a prince and heir to the British throne was officially announced on Tuesday forenoon, bv the publication of the London Gazelle Extraordinary, ol which the following is a copy : þÿ Buckingham Palack, Nov. 9. " This morning, at twelve minutes before eleven, the Queen was happily delivered of a prince. His Royal Highness Prince Albert, her Royal Highness the Duchess of Kent, several Lords of her Majesty's Most Honorable Privy Council, and the ladies of her Majesty's bedchamber, being present. " This great and important news was immediately made known to the town by the firing of the Park and Tower guns; and the Privy Council being assembled as soon as possible thereupon, at the Council Chamber, Whitehall, it was ordered that a form of thanksgiving for the Queen's sale delivery of a prince be prepared by his grace the Archbishop of Canterbury, to be used in all churches and chapels throughout England and Wales, and the town of Berwick upon-Twecd, on Sundav, the 14th of November, or the Sunday after the respective ministers shall receive the same. " Her Majesty and the infant Prince are, " God be praised, both doing well This important event produced afar greater degree of joyous excitement than has been exhibited on any occasion within the memory of the oldest inhabitant of the metropolis. The Cth of November þÿ Lord Mayor's Day. as it is familiarly termed þÿ is ever held,

amongst the citizens of London at least, as a day of jubilee. It was yesterday converted into one universal holiday by all classes and conditions of her Majesty's subjects. The auspicious event, although daily anticipated for the past fortnight, has come upon the country with a pleasurable sudden sur. prise ; and those gratelul emotions are considerably enhanced bv the official announcement with which the Gazelle Extraordinary concludes : þÿ " Her Majesty and the infant Prince are. God be praised, both doing well.'' Her Majesty's accouchement took place (as stated in the Gazelle Extraordinary) at ten minutes past eleven o'clock a m. There were in the royal chamber at the time, the Prince Albert, the Duchess of Kent, the Archbishop of Canterbury, the Lord Chancellor, Sir Robert Peel, the Bishop of London, the Duke of Wellington, the Lord Chamberlain, the Lord Steward, the Ladies in Wailing, the medical attendants, and M rs. I ,illv, the monthly nurse. The other ministers and principal officers and ladies of the household were admitted to the ante room. The sex of the royal infant was announced by Sir James Clark to the anxious group of distinguished personages assembled in the royal chamber, and subsequently to those collected in the ante room, exciting in every bosom unspeakable emotions of joy and gratitude. Prince Albeit received the congratulationsappropriute to the occasion with graceful alfabilily. The union jack was hoisted from the steeples of the several parish churches, and the
Park and Tower guns fired royal salutes,

The Duke of Wellington looked in better health and in higher spirits than lor many years past. Alter the Council had broken up, his grace, who went on horseback to the Palace, entered the Park through the Horse Guards-gate, and meeting with t lie Earl ol Liverpool, who was on fool, his giace alighted, and giving his horse to the groom, took the Earl ot Liverpool's arm, and walked across the Park, followed by an immense concourse of persons, who cheered his grace most vehemently all the way up, Constitution-hill, and until he entered Apsley House. The Duke frequently acknowledged the congratulations ot the multitude, and seemed pleased with the spontaneous fervour of their enthusiasm.

In the evening the national anthem was sung at most of the patent and minor I Ilea ires, and was received with every demonstration ollloyalty At the lioval Surrey Theatre the following additional stanza of the National Anthem, written on the moment, was sung with extraordinary client on the audience crowded to the celling ; þÿ ' Oh God, bless thou this day, That Prince was born to sway Old England's throne ; Triumph his steps attend, Sweet peace her blessings lend, Make him the people's friend, þÿ God bless our Prince."

At the Adelphi Theatre, when the perform ance was brought to a conclusion, the entire company came on the stage and sang the national anthem ; the tollovving additional verse, extemporised for the occasion bv Mi. Plunkelt, being given in excellent styie by Mis. Graltan ; þÿ " Oh, Lord, in bounty shed Joys round the Inlant's head : þÿ j selected Shield him from harm. Hear now a nation's prayer, Guard England's youthful heir, Make him thy special care þÿ God save the Queen." Nothing could exceed the enthusiastic acclamation with which the last verse was received, and the manifestations of lovaltv and joy displayed by the audience in all parts of the house exceeded anything we have ever witnessed. Many of the tradesmen of the metropolis testified their loyalty towatds her Majesty, ! malic of the peace which was then about to and their joy upon the truly auspicious event ol the birth ol a Prince, by illuminating their houses. Although the time for preparing the lamps, erecting the apparatus, Ate., was short, some of the illuminations were tasteful, if not magnificent. i The rejoicings in the country, on itie birth of the prince, and the well doing of her Majesty, we are happy to say lias been universal throughout the kingdom, and simultaneous meetings have been held to deliberate on the propriety of some suitable demonstration of loyalty on this auspicious occasion.

Sir Thomas Wilde and Mr. Martin, were retained by the pitsoner to conduct his defence. Mr. Clarke (the Clerk of Arraigns), then read the indictment, which is of considerable leng'h. It charged the prisoner that he, Edward Beaumont Smith did on the Kith of October last, in the parish of St. Martin's. inthe f ields, feloniously forge a certain Exchequer-bill bearing date the 16fh of June, 1841, and numbered f!405, for the sunt of 1000/. a charge of felony ; what have you to sav why the court should not pass sentence upon you according to law ?" lie was then ordered to fie brought up for judgment, and spoke as follows : þÿ I pray your lordship's indulgence while 1 ofler a few words to your consideration before you discharge the duty which mv conduct has imposed upon you. that of passing sentence upon me. 1 would have received that sen 'ence in respectful silence, and have thereby

The crime 1 have committed is great. 1 do not attempt to excuse or extenuate it, but it will not be forgotten that I have submitted myself to meet and exclusively to bear all the consequences of that crime, and have not sought to screen myself by the addition of duplicity or meanness, and 1 respectfully implore the court not to think that I do not feel all the weight and enormity of the otlence itself, because I humblv call its attention to circumstances which are calculated to show that 1 have not become altogether debased in my feelings and principles Pecuniary difficulty, arising from misplaced confidence, and unconnected w ith discredit, and of very limited extent, not exceeding a few hundred pounds, although beyond my means to meet, first exposed me to the suggestions of those who tempted me to obtain a temporary relict by the fraudulent fabrication of Exchequer-bills, to be pledged for a short time, and then to be redeemed and cancelled for ever. 1 yielded to the temptation, but without obtaining the promised relief, and once committed, I became in the power of the tempter, and my retreat has been prevented. Allured and beguiled by plausibility, power, and talent,

which I could not resist, J became entangled beyond escape and while Exchequer-bills were obtained trom me to an enormous extent, I never derived benefit even to the small extent necessary to relieve me from mv comparatively trifling embarrassments, and 1 am at this moment in debt for money actually borrowed from sources unconnected with Exchequer hills topay off my original incumbrances A sordid or avaricious motive has never influenced me, and I have been sacrificed to the object of others. The foreign intelligence of the past week is of more variety than importance ; France and Spain are the only heads, there having been no at rivals worth mentioning from America and the East In France, up to the time we write, the only subject of interest is the successful effort of the government to comprehend M. Dupoty, the editor of the radical and irreligious paper, the Journal du People. within the expected condemnation of Quenisset's trial The object of the government, and chiefly of the King personally, is to procure the exemplary punishment of a ruffian who most richly de serves it ; I )u poi v being one of the worst men in a nation of had men, and his paper, the Journal du P> uple, being the most conspicuous firebrand amongst so many other papers, which arc all alike torches of sedition. There is no intelligence from Spain of any interest ; the papers are full of the miserable state ot the country, and of the insecurity of persons and property from the outrages of the armed brigands who infest every part.
